common_name: Cambridge Gage Plum (Small Sweet English Gage-Type Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; partially self-fertile but sets heavier crops with a nearby European plum pollinizer, and is best adapted to zones 5-8.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune annually to an open-center form. Cambridge Gage is an English selection from the historic gage family of European plums descended from the original Reine Claude, producing small, round, greenish-gold fruit with the same rich, exceptionally sweet, honeyed flavor that made the original Green Gage famous, in a somewhat more reliably productive tree than some other gage selections. The delicate skin and juicy, tender flesh make it best suited to fresh eating and preserves rather than heavy handling or long-distance shipping, since fruit bruises easily once ripe. Harvest when fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure and the green skin has softened toward gold, and use promptly, since gage-type plums typically have a short window of peak ripeness.

common_name: Denniston's Superb Plum (Cold-Hardy American Gage-Type Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit, and is well adapted to zones 4-8.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit, though a nearby pollinizer can improve yields. Denniston's Superb is an early 1800s American gage-type plum bred for cold hardiness and reliable self-fertility, two practical advantages over many European gage selections that need cross-pollination and struggle in harsher climates. The medium, round, greenish-yellow fruit has dense, sweet, richly flavored flesh in the classic gage tradition, good for both fresh eating and preserves. The vigorous, hardy tree bears reliably once established, making it a solid choice for northern home orchardists who want good gage-type flavor without the fussier pollination and hardiness requirements of some European varieties. Harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure and has fully colored.

common_name: Jefferson Plum (Fine-Flavored American Golden Gage-Type Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; partially self-fertile but sets heavier crops with a nearby European plum pollinizer, and is best adapted to zones 5-8.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune annually to an open-center form. Jefferson was raised in New York in the 1820s and became one of the most highly regarded American plums of the 19th century, producing large, golden-yellow fruit blushed with red and carrying rich, sweet, aromatic flesh often compared favorably to the classic European gage plums it descends from. The vigorous tree crops reliably and the large fruit size, combined with outstanding flavor, made it a standard for fine dessert plums in American orchards for generations. Thin fruit if a heavy crop sets to maintain good size, and harvest once fruit yields to gentle pressure and has fully colored for the best flavor, since Jefferson plums picked too early lack the full richness the variety is known for.

common_name: Purple Pershore Plum (Classic English Cooking and Jam Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit, and is best adapted to zones 5-8.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit. Purple Pershore takes its name from the English town of Pershore in Worcestershire, historically the center of a major English plum-growing and jam-making industry built substantially around this variety, prized for consistently heavy crops of small to medium, deep purple, tart-fleshed fruit that cooks down into excellent jam, chutney, and stewed plum preparations. The fruit is generally considered too tart and firm for fresh eating out of hand but excels once cooked with sugar, developing rich, deep plum flavor that made it a commercial jam standard for generations in England. The tree is notably reliable and productive, an important trait for a variety grown primarily for volume processing rather than fresh market appeal; harvest once fruit fully colors and yields slightly to pressure.
